purpose: Security boundaries for authenticated user sessions and account-sensitive actions across Shine applications.
requirements: Authentication and authorisation decisions are enforced server-side; client state, hidden controls or route visibility are never treated as authority.
Session identifiers and one-time authentication tokens are cryptographically unpredictable, purpose-bound and never accepted from URL query strings.
Cookie-backed sessions use HttpOnly cookies and production transport requires Secure cookies; SameSite and Path scope are set deliberately for the application flow.
Session state has explicit idle and absolute expiry, and expiry is enforced by the server rather than inferred only by the client.
Sessions are rotated after authentication and meaningful privilege changes so pre-authentication session identifiers do not survive elevation.
Logout, credential reset, account disablement and membership revocation invalidate relevant server-side session or refresh state promptly.
Cookie-authenticated state-changing requests are protected against cross-site submission with origin/host checks and an explicit CSRF strategy appropriate to the architecture.

Login, recovery, verification, invitation and other credential-bearing endpoints use bounded request bodies, input validation, abuse throttling and generic failure responses that avoid account enumeration.
Password reset, email verification, invitation and similar one-time tokens are short-lived, single-purpose and invalid after successful use or replacement.
Redirect and return-to destinations are constrained to reviewed local paths or explicit allowlists so authentication flows cannot become open redirects.
Privileged service credentials remain separate from end-user session credentials and are not exposed to browser code or logs.
Authentication, revocation and sensitive account-change events create security-relevant audit evidence without storing raw passwords, session identifiers, bearer tokens or reset secrets.
When the authentication or authorisation dependency cannot establish a trustworthy decision, protected operations fail closed.
nonClaims: This policy does not prove a person's real-world identity.
This policy does not guarantee that an account can never be compromised.
This policy does not substitute for application-specific authorisation rules, data-scoping checks or least-privilege design.
This policy does not claim multi-factor authentication unless the application separately implements and verifies it.
